The first thing most people notice when they step into a temperate rainforest is not a particular tree or animal but a quality of the air. It is cool, heavy, and faintly sweet, carrying the smell of wet bark, decaying wood, and the green mineral scent that rises from moss after rain. Sound behaves differently here. Footsteps are swallowed by a carpet of needles and bryophytes, birdsong seems to come from everywhere and nowhere, and the dominant noise is often water: dripping from branches, trickling through root channels, running in creeks the color of weak tea. Light arrives filtered and broken, tinted green by the leaves and mosses it passes through before reaching the forest floor. To understand these forests, which are among the rarest and most biologically remarkable ecosystems on Earth, it helps to learn to read these sensory clues as evidence of the processes that shape them. This guide is an attempt to teach that kind of reading, moving from the broad climatic conditions that make temperate rainforests possible down to the logs, lichens, fungi, and animals that a careful observer might encounter on a single afternoon's walk.

Temperate rainforests are defined less by any single species than by a combination of climatic circumstances. Ecologists have proposed various thresholds, but the most widely used working definition describes forests in the mid-latitudes that receive abundant precipitation, commonly more than 1,400 millimeters a year and often far more, that experience relatively mild temperatures without extreme heat or prolonged hard freezing, and, critically, that have a substantial share of their rainfall during the summer or are bathed in summer fog and cloud. That last condition matters enormously. Many places receive heavy winter rain but bake dry in summer, and those landscapes tend toward fire-adapted woodlands and chaparral. A true temperate rainforest stays damp through the growing season, and that persistent moisture allows organisms that cannot tolerate desiccation, such as many mosses, liverworts, filmy ferns, and lichens, to flourish on every available surface. The result is a forest in which the boundary between ground and tree, living and dead, becomes blurred under layers of green.

Such conditions arise in only a handful of places, almost always where moist air from a cool ocean meets a coastal mountain range. As westerly winds push maritime air inland, the mountains force it upward, where it cools and releases its moisture as rain, drizzle, and fog. This orographic effect explains why temperate rainforests cling to the western edges of continents in the mid-latitudes of both hemispheres. The largest expanse lies along the Pacific coast of North America, stretching in a discontinuous band from northern California through Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia to southeastern Alaska, where it gives way to boreal and subalpine forest around Prince William Sound and Kodiak. In the Southern Hemisphere, the Valdivian and Magellanic forests of southern Chile and adjacent Argentina form the second great block. Smaller but significant areas occur in Tasmania and southeastern mainland Australia, on the western side of New Zealand's South Island and in parts of the North Island, on the western coast of Norway, in the oceanic fringes of Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and southwestern England, in the Colchic forests along the eastern Black Sea in Georgia and northeastern Turkey, in parts of Japan and Korea, and in a few interior locations such as the inland rainforests of British Columbia's Columbia and Rocky Mountains, which receive moisture from deep winter snowpacks and summer storms rather than directly from the sea. Taken together, these forests cover only a small fraction of the world's forested land, a percentage usually estimated in the low single digits, and much of what remains has been logged, fragmented, or converted.

The geographic scattering of temperate rainforests means that an observer who knows the forests of Vancouver Island will find the trees of Chiloé or Tasmania entirely unfamiliar at the species level. Yet the ecological patterns repeat with uncanny consistency. In each region, one finds tall, long-lived trees; an enormous accumulation of biomass both living and dead; heavy loads of epiphytes; slow decomposition and abundant woody debris; nutrient-limited soils; and complex relationships between forest and stream. Learning these shared patterns is the core of field ecology in these places, and it allows a naturalist to move between continents with a framework that makes new species legible.

Begin with the trees, because they are the architecture on which everything else depends. In the Pacific Northwest, the signature canopy species are conifers. Sitka spruce dominates the narrow fog belt nearest the ocean, a tree with stiff, sharp needles that prick the hand when grasped, bark that flakes off in thin purplish-gray scales, and a tolerance for salt spray that lets it stand at the very edge of the sea. Western hemlock, perhaps the most characteristic tree of the region, is recognizable from a distance by its drooping leader, the topmost shoot that nods like a tired head, and close up by its short, flat needles of unequal length that give branches a feathery, lacy look. Western redcedar, which is not a true cedar but a member of the cypress family, has fibrous, reddish bark that peels in long strips and scale-like leaves arranged in flattened sprays; turn a spray over and you will often see faint white markings on the underside resembling tiny butterflies or bowties. Douglas-fir, a tree that depends on disturbance and full sunlight for regeneration, persists in many rainforest stands as a legacy of fires centuries ago, its deeply furrowed, corky bark rising in columns among the hemlocks and cedars. Farther south in California, coast redwood occupies a comparable ecological position within the fog belt, drawing a significant portion of its summer water from fog intercepted by its foliage and dripping to the ground, and even absorbing some moisture directly through its leaves.

These trees are giants. Sitka spruce and coast redwood can exceed eighty meters in height, and redwoods hold the record for the tallest living trees, with individuals topping one hundred and fifteen meters. Western redcedars may live well over a thousand years and develop trunk diameters of several meters. The great stature and longevity of these conifers is not an accident. In a climate where winters are mild and wet, evergreen conifers can photosynthesize during much of the year, accumulating carbon slowly but persistently, while their dry summers are moderated by fog and cloud. Over centuries, this produces forests with some of the highest standing biomass recorded on Earth, exceeding even that of most tropical rainforests on a per-hectare basis. When ecologists measure carbon stocks, old-growth stands in the Pacific Northwest consistently rank among the most carbon-dense ecosystems anywhere.

In the Southern Hemisphere, the canopy looks very different. Southern beeches of the genus Nothofagus dominate much of the temperate rainforest of Chile, Argentina, Tasmania, mainland Australia, and New Zealand. Their distribution across landmasses now separated by thousands of kilometers of ocean is one of the classic illustrations of the ancient supercontinent Gondwana, though the biogeographic story is more complex than simple vicariance, involving some long-distance dispersal as well. Fossil Nothofagus pollen has even been found in Antarctica, a reminder that these forests once grew on a continent now buried in ice. In Tasmania, myrtle beech forms dense, evergreen stands with small, toothed, dark-green leaves, often accompanied by sassafras, celery-top pine, and leatherwood, a tree whose white summer flowers produce a distinctive honey. In New Zealand, beech forests share the landscape with towering podocarps, a group of conifers that includes rimu, kahikatea, tōtara, and miro, many of which bear fleshy, brightly colored seed structures rather than cones. In southern Chile, the Valdivian rainforest mixes evergreen southern beeches like coigüe with broadleaf trees such as ulmo and tepa, along with conifers that include the extraordinary alerce, Fitzroya cupressoides, a close ecological counterpart to the redwoods. Alerce trees can live for more than three thousand years; one individual has been estimated to approach or exceed five thousand years by some researchers, though such claims remain debated. Exploited for centuries for its rot-resistant wood, alerce is now legally protected in Chile as a natural monument.

The European temperate rainforests, often called Atlantic or Celtic rainforests, look different again. Here the canopy is often formed by sessile oak, downy birch, ash, rowan, holly, and hazel, trees that a visitor might find unremarkable in a drier woodland. What makes these places rainforests is not the trees themselves but what grows upon them. Along the western coasts of Scotland, Ireland, Wales, and Cornwall, high rainfall spread across many days of the year and mild winters allow a profusion of oceanic mosses, liverworts, ferns, and lichens that are rare or absent elsewhere in Europe. A gnarled oak in a Scottish glen may be draped so thoroughly in Isothecium mosses and polypody ferns that its bark is invisible. The Colchic forests of the Caucasus contain oriental beech, chestnut-leaved oak, Caucasian wingnut, and an evergreen understory of cherry laurel and Pontic rhododendron, some of them relicts of a once more widespread Tertiary flora. In Japan, the rainforests of Yakushima, with their ancient Japanese cedars, or sugi, some reputed to be thousands of years old, carry a mossy richness that has inspired artists and filmmakers.

Once you can recognize the dominant trees of a given forest, the next step is to look at how they are arranged. Old-growth temperate rainforests are structurally complex. Rather than a uniform canopy of trees of similar age, a mature stand contains trees of many sizes and ages, standing dead trees called snags, fallen logs in various stages of decay, multilayered canopies, and gaps where light reaches the floor. This complexity is the product of time and of the particular way these forests are disturbed. In many temperate rainforests, especially those near the coast, large stand-replacing fires are rare, occurring at intervals of many centuries or not at all. Instead, the most frequent disturbances are small: a single tree snapped by wind, a cluster of trees uprooted in a winter storm, a patch killed by root disease or insects. Ecologists call this gap-phase dynamics. When a large tree falls, it opens a hole in the canopy, and the sudden pulse of light allows suppressed saplings that have waited for decades in the shade to grow rapidly toward the sky. Over time, the forest becomes a mosaic of patches at different stages of recovery, each the record of a particular fall.

Windthrow has a distinctive signature that a careful observer can learn to spot. When a shallow-rooted tree topples, it lifts a great plate of roots and soil out of the ground, leaving a depression called a pit and creating, as the root plate decays and collapses, an adjacent hummock called a mound. The landscape of many old rainforests is pocked with these pit-and-mound features, some fresh and raw, others so old they are smoothed into gentle undulations covered in moss. The pits collect water and organic matter; the mounds expose mineral soil and drain quickly. Together they create microhabitats with different moisture and nutrient conditions, adding to the diversity of plants and fungi on the forest floor. In Southeast Alaska, where wind is the dominant disturbance, researchers have shown that windthrow patterns vary with topography and exposure, so that some slopes are repeatedly disturbed while sheltered valleys may go centuries without significant blowdown, producing forests of very different structure within short distances.

Not all temperate rainforests escape fire, and the role of fire varies considerably. Douglas-fir stands in the Cascades and parts of Washington's Olympic Peninsula bear the imprint of large fires centuries ago, and in Tasmania and Victoria the boundary between rainforest and fire-prone eucalypt forest is dynamic, shifting with the history of burning. Some of the tallest flowering plants on Earth, the mountain ash eucalypts of Victoria and Tasmania, typically grow over a rainforest understory of myrtle beech and tree ferns and depend on intense fire for regeneration. Where fire returns too frequently, rainforest species may be eliminated; where fire is long absent, the eucalypts eventually die out and rainforest takes over. Similar tensions exist in Chile, where human-set fires have pushed back rainforest boundaries and where some forest types, including some alerce stands, have been severely damaged by burning. Knowing a region's fire history is therefore essential to interpreting what you see. A stand of uniform-aged Douglas-fir with scattered charred snags tells a very different story from a multi-aged hemlock and cedar forest with no trace of charcoal in the soil.

Look down from the canopy to the ground and you will find one of the most important features of temperate rainforest ecology: dead wood. In an old-growth Pacific Northwest forest, fallen logs and standing snags can amount to hundreds of tonnes per hectare, and the forest floor may be so crisscrossed with logs that walking off-trail means climbing over trunks every few meters. To the untrained eye this may look like waste or disorder. To an ecologist it is one of the forest's great reservoirs of habitat, water, nutrients, and carbon.

Because temperatures are cool and conditions often waterlogged, decomposition in temperate rainforests is slow. A large Douglas-fir or redcedar log may take several centuries to fully decay, and some redcedar wood, rich in natural fungicidal compounds called thujaplicins, resists rot for a very long time. During that slow decay, a log passes through a sequence of stages that ecologists classify by the condition of bark, branches, wood texture, and shape. A freshly fallen log retains its bark and small twigs and sits on the ground supported by branches. As it ages, the bark sloughs off, the twigs vanish, and the wood softens, first in the sapwood and then deeper. Eventually the log loses its round cross-section, slumps into an oval and then into a soft, moss-covered ridge of reddish-brown material that can be broken apart by hand, and finally merges with the soil, sometimes leaving only a raised line of moss and seedlings to mark where a tree once lay.

Each stage hosts different organisms. Bark beetles and wood-boring beetles colonize early, carrying fungal spores into the wood as they tunnel. Fungi then begin the hard chemical work of breaking down cellulose and lignin, the tough structural compounds of wood. Brown-rot fungi primarily attack cellulose, leaving behind crumbly, cubical, reddish-brown residues rich in lignin that persist in soils for long periods and help retain water. White-rot fungi can degrade lignin as well, leaving wood pale, stringy, and spongy. Carpenter ants, termites in some regions, mites, springtails, and countless other invertebrates follow, along with the predators that hunt them, from centipedes to salamanders. In the Pacific Northwest, ensatina and clouded salamanders shelter in and beneath decaying logs, and the moist interior of a well-rotted log may serve as a refuge during dry spells. Small mammals such as red-backed voles and shrews use logs as runways and nesting sites. A single large log may support hundreds of species over its lifetime.

Rotting logs also serve as nurseries for new trees. In the dense, moss-covered forest floor of many temperate rainforests, a tiny conifer seedling has a hard time establishing itself. The moss layer can be thick enough to smother seedlings, the ground may be covered with competing herbs and shrubs, and soil-borne pathogenic fungi may kill germinants. A decaying log offers an elevated, moist, relatively competition-free seedbed. Western hemlock and Sitka spruce seedlings are especially likely to germinate on such logs, which are therefore called nurse logs. Over decades, the young trees send roots down over the sides of the log to reach the soil. When the log eventually rots away completely, the trees it nurtured are left standing in a straight line, their bases raised on stilt-like roots that arch over the empty space once occupied by the log. A row of trees standing on stilts is one of the most legible pieces of history in the forest, telling you that a large tree fell here perhaps two or three centuries ago. Similar processes occur on stumps, which become nurse stumps, and in New Zealand and Chile, where seedlings of many species exploit fallen trunks and the bases of tree ferns.

Dead wood also links forests to rivers. When large trees fall into streams, they shape channels in ways that were poorly understood until the second half of the twentieth century, when researchers in the Pacific Northwest began documenting the consequences of removing woody debris from streams for log drives, navigation, or under the mistaken belief that it impeded fish. Large wood creates pools, traps gravel and sediment, slows water, diversifies flow, and provides cover for fish. Logjams can store sediment for decades, building gravel bars and side channels that juvenile salmon use for rearing. A stream without wood tends to be simplified, faster, and poorer in habitat. Today, restoring large wood to streams is a standard practice in salmon recovery efforts, and a naturalist walking along a rainforest creek should pay attention to how logs bend, split, and pool the water, as these structures are central to the aquatic ecology.

That connection between forest and stream runs in both directions, and nowhere more dramatically than with Pacific salmon. Each year, millions of salmon return from the ocean to spawn in the rivers and streams that drain coastal rainforests from California to Alaska. Having spent years feeding at sea, they carry with them nutrients accumulated in marine food webs, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus. After spawning, the fish die, and their bodies decompose in and along streams. Bears, wolves, eagles, gulls, ravens, river otters, mink, and a host of invertebrates feed on the carcasses, and bears in particular often carry salmon away from the water to eat in the forest, leaving partially consumed remains among the trees. Researchers using stable isotope analysis have found that marine-derived nitrogen, which has a distinctive isotopic signature, can be traced into riparian vegetation, insects, songbirds, and even the growth rings of streamside trees. Studies in British Columbia and Alaska have documented relationships between salmon abundance and the nitrogen signatures, composition, and productivity of streamside plant communities. In effect, the ocean fertilizes the forest, and the forest, by providing shade, wood, and clean gravel, sustains the fish that carry the ocean inland. When observing a salmon stream in autumn, notice the trampled paths along the banks, the scattered fish skeletons in the moss, and the gathering of scavengers, and you will be watching one of the great nutrient transfers in temperate ecosystems.

The fact that salmon-derived nutrients can measurably affect forests points to an important truth about temperate rainforests: despite their lush appearance, many are nutrient-limited. Heavy rainfall leaches soluble nutrients from soils, and slow decomposition locks a large proportion of nitrogen and other elements in organic matter rather than in forms available to plants. Many rainforest soils are acidic and covered by thick organic horizons. In wetter, flatter areas, especially in Southeast Alaska and coastal British Columbia, poor drainage leads to the development of peatlands, called muskegs in Alaska, and to the gradual transformation of forest into bog over long periods through a process known as paludification, in which accumulating mosses and waterlogged organic material raise the water table and stunt trees. Walk from a productive valley-bottom forest up onto a gently sloping bench and you may see trees shrink into scattered, stunted shore pine and yellow-cedar, the ground becoming a squelching carpet of Sphagnum moss, sundews, and sedges. These muskegs are part of the rainforest mosaic, and their presence reflects the limits that water and nutrients place on tree growth.

In such nutrient-poor environments, the relationships between plants and fungi become crucial. The great majority of trees in temperate rainforests form mycorrhizal associations, symbiotic partnerships in which fungal threads called hyphae grow on or within plant roots. The fungi extend far into the soil, exploring a volume no root could reach, absorbing water, nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients, and passing some of them to the plant. In exchange, the plant supplies the fungus with sugars produced through photosynthesis. Conifers such as Douglas-fir, hemlock, and spruce, along with southern beeches, typically form ectomycorrhizae, in which the fungus wraps the root tips in a sheath and grows between root cells. Redcedar and many understory plants form arbuscular mycorrhizae, in which the fungus penetrates root cells. The mushrooms you see in autumn, such as chanterelles, boletes, russulas, and the scarlet-capped fly agaric in some regions, are often the fruiting bodies of ectomycorrhizal fungi, the visible tip of a vast underground network.

Considerable research and public interest have focused on whether these networks connect trees to one another and allow the transfer of carbon, water, or signals between individuals, an idea popularized under phrases like the wood wide web. Experiments in forests of western North America have shown that mycorrhizal fungi can link the roots of multiple trees and that some movement of carbon and nutrients through these connections can occur. However, the extent and ecological significance of such transfers remain actively debated, and several recent reviews have argued that popular accounts have overstated the evidence, particularly claims that mother trees deliberately nurture their offspring or that forests function as cooperative communities. A careful naturalist can appreciate the reality that fungi and trees are deeply interdependent, and that the soil beneath any rainforest is threaded with kilometers of hyphae, without committing to the more speculative interpretations.

Some fungi have relationships that are even stranger. Certain plants in temperate rainforests have abandoned photosynthesis altogether and obtain their carbon from fungi, which in turn obtain it from trees. In the Pacific Northwest, the ghostly white ghost plant or Indian pipe, Monotropa uniflora, and the striped candy-cane plant Allotropa virgata are examples of such mycoheterotrophs. Their lack of chlorophyll gives them a pale, unearthly appearance, and finding them in the deep shade of an old-growth stand is a quiet reminder of how fully the forest's economy runs through its fungal networks. Truffle-forming fungi, which fruit underground, depend on animals to disperse their spores. In the Pacific Northwest, northern flying squirrels and red-backed voles dig up and eat truffles, then defecate spores elsewhere, spreading fungi that the trees require. The flying squirrel in turn is a principal prey of the northern spotted owl, linking a threatened raptor to underground fungi through a chain of dependencies. In Australia and Tasmania, small marsupials called bettongs and potoroos play similar roles as truffle eaters.

Above ground, one of the defining features of temperate rainforests is the abundance of epiphytes, plants and other organisms that grow on other plants without parasitizing them. In tropical rainforests, epiphytes are often flowering plants such as orchids and bromeliads. In temperate rainforests, mosses, liverworts, lichens, and ferns dominate. The density of these communities can be astonishing. In the Hoh and Queets valleys of Washington's Olympic Peninsula, bigleaf maples are clothed in such thick mats of moss and licorice fern that the branches appear swollen, and the epiphytes on a single large maple can weigh far more than the tree's own leaves. Studies in these forests have found that epiphyte biomass in old-growth canopies can be several tonnes per hectare.

Over time, the accumulated epiphytes, along with trapped debris and decomposing organic matter, form what ecologists call canopy soils, layers of humus-like material on branches high above the ground. These arboreal soils can be several centimeters thick and support their own communities of invertebrates, fungi, and microbes. Remarkably, some trees, including bigleaf maple and certain tropical species, can produce roots from their branches that grow into these canopy soils and draw nutrients from them, effectively tapping a second, elevated soil. This discovery, made by researchers climbing into the canopies of Olympic Peninsula forests, changed how ecologists think about nutrient cycling in these systems. The canopy is not merely a collection of leaves but a habitat with its own processes.

Lichens deserve special attention because they are often overlooked yet profoundly important. A lichen is a partnership, traditionally described as a fungus living with a photosynthetic partner, either a green alga or a cyanobacterium. Research in the past decade has complicated that picture, revealing that many lichens also contain additional fungal partners, particularly yeasts, so that a lichen is better understood as a small community than a pair. In temperate rainforests, some lichens contain cyanobacteria capable of fixing atmospheric nitrogen, converting it into forms usable by living things. Among the most important of these is Lobaria oregana, sometimes called lettuce lichen, a large, leafy, pale-green lichen with ridged lobes that grows abundantly in the upper canopies of old-growth Douglas-fir forests in the Pacific Northwest. As these lichens fall to the ground in storms and decompose, or as nitrogen leaches from them in rainwater, they contribute a meaningful share of the nitrogen entering the forest ecosystem, a significant subsidy in a nitrogen-poor environment. Its relative, Lobaria pulmonaria, known as lungwort because its lobed, ridged surface was once thought to resemble lung tissue, is widespread in old forests across the Northern Hemisphere and is often regarded as an indicator of long ecological continuity in European woodlands.

That idea of ecological continuity is worth dwelling on. Many epiphytic lichens and bryophytes disperse slowly and establish poorly, so they are found mainly in forests that have remained wooded for very long periods. In the Atlantic rainforests of Britain and Ireland, communities of lichens such as Lobaria species, along with specialized liverworts and oceanic mosses, are used as indicators of ancient woodland. The so-called Lobarion community, an assemblage of large leafy lichens including Lobaria and Sticta species, is characteristic of clean-air, humid, long-continuous woodlands and has declined across much of Europe because of air pollution and habitat loss. On hazel stems in western Scotland, observers may find a mosaic of small, colorful crust lichens, some of them rare on a global scale, as well as the curious hazel gloves fungus, Hypocreopsis rhododendri, which forms clusters of orange-brown finger-like lobes on old hazel and is considered a flagship species of these Celtic rainforests. Learning to recognize even a handful of indicator lichens transforms a walk in such woods into a kind of historical reading, since the presence of these organisms suggests that the site has offered stable conditions for a long time.

Lichens are also exquisitely sensitive to air quality. Many species, particularly those with cyanobacterial partners and large, leafy or shrubby forms, are damaged by sulfur dioxide, nitrogen compounds, and other pollutants. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, industrial pollution stripped lichens from woods across much of Europe. In the Pacific Northwest, lichen surveys are used as biological monitors of nitrogen deposition and air pollution. A forest whose trees bear long, hanging strands of Usnea or Alectoria lichens, often called old man's beard or witch's hair, and abundant leafy Lobaria is likely breathing clean air. In Pacific Northwest forests, the hair lichens also serve as winter food for black-tailed deer and, farther inland in the interior wet belt of British Columbia, for mountain caribou, which depend heavily on arboreal lichens in old forests during deep-snow winters. The decline of these caribou herds has been tied in part to logging of old-growth interior rainforests and the resulting changes in predator-prey dynamics.

Mosses and liverworts form the green fabric of the temperate rainforest floor and bark. In the Pacific Northwest, step moss, Hylocomium splendens, builds feathery, stair-stepped fronds that add a new segment each year, so that counting the steps provides a rough age. Oregon beaked moss, Kindbergia oregana, and cat-tail moss, Isothecium myosuroides, drape trunks and branches. Large, glossy mounds of Rhytidiadelphus mosses cover logs. In New Zealand, the forest floor and tree trunks are home to an extraordinary diversity of bryophytes, among them Dawsonia superba, one of the tallest mosses in the world, which can grow to half a meter. Southern Chile likewise has a rich bryophyte and filmy fern flora. Filmy ferns, members of the family Hymenophyllaceae, have fronds only one cell thick, making them translucent and extremely vulnerable to drying; they flourish only where humidity remains consistently high and so are among the most reliable indicators of genuine rainforest conditions. Seeing a trunk coated with filmy ferns tells you that the air here seldom dries out.

The importance of these small plants goes beyond aesthetics. Moss mats act like sponges, absorbing and storing large quantities of rainwater and releasing it slowly, moderating streamflow and humidity. They provide habitat for tardigrades, rotifers, nematodes, mites, and springtails, often in staggering numbers. Some mosses host nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria; in boreal forests, feather mosses associated with cyanobacteria contribute substantially to nitrogen inputs, and similar associations occur in some temperate rainforest settings. Mosses also influence which seedlings can establish, insulate soils, and slow the evaporation of water from the forest floor.

Ferns are another conspicuous element. In the Pacific Northwest, sword fern, with its tough, evergreen fronds and small, hilt-like projections at the base of each leaflet, carpets the floor of many lowland forests. Deer fern, with its distinct sterile and fertile fronds, the latter narrow and upright, marks wetter and more acidic sites. Lady fern grows in moist openings, and licorice fern grows epiphytically on mossy maple branches, its rhizome tasting faintly sweet. In Tasmania, Victoria, New Zealand, and Chile, tree ferns add a strikingly different texture. The soft tree fern, Dicksonia antarctica, of southeastern Australia and Tasmania grows a fibrous trunk that is in fact a mass of matted roots surrounding the stem, and that trunk serves as a seedbed for other ferns, mosses, and even tree seedlings. New Zealand's silver fern, ponga, with its silvery-white underside, is a national emblem, and the islands host several species of tree ferns that rise above the shrub layer to form a distinctive subcanopy. A walk through such a forest gives the impression of something ancient, and indeed ferns and their relatives represent lineages that long predate flowering plants, though most modern tree fern species are not themselves unchanged relicts.

The understory shrubs of temperate rainforests often bear berries, and they provide food for birds and mammals and, historically and today, for people. In coastal British Columbia and Alaska, salal forms dense thickets with leathery, glossy leaves and dark purple berries that were a staple food for many Indigenous peoples. Red huckleberry grows on stumps and logs, its bright red berries glowing against green moss. Salmonberry, whose name may derive from its berries' salmon-like colors or from being eaten with salmon, flowers early in spring with magenta blossoms that attract hummingbirds just as rufous hummingbirds return from the south. Devil's club, a tall shrub in the ginseng family, has enormous maple-like leaves and stems covered in sharp spines, and it grows thickly in wet, seepy ground along streams. Anyone who has grabbed a devil's club stem while slipping on a slope will remember the lesson. Despite its hostility, it is a valued medicinal plant in many Indigenous traditions of the Northwest coast. In Chile, the understory may include chusquea bamboos, which form impenetrable thickets and flower synchronously at long intervals, followed by mass dieback, an event that can trigger rodent population explosions as the animals feast on the abundant seed.

Turn now to the animals. Temperate rainforests are not known for spectacular species richness the way tropical forests are, but they host a remarkable number of endemic, specialized, and ancient creatures, many of them closely tied to old-growth structure. In the Pacific Northwest, the banana slug, Ariolimax, is the forest floor's unofficial mascot. These large, yellow or olive slugs, sometimes spotted with black, can exceed twenty centimeters in length. They feed on fallen leaves, fungi, animal droppings, and plant material, playing an important role in decomposition and nutrient cycling, and they disperse the seeds and spores of some plants and fungi. Their slime, a complex mucus, helps them move, retain moisture, and deter predators, and it can anesthetize the tongue of animals that try to eat them. Watch for them on damp mornings and after rain, especially along trails and on mossy logs.

Amphibians are particularly characteristic of temperate rainforests, because the persistent moisture allows species with permeable skin to live well away from open water. The Pacific Northwest supports a distinctive suite of salamanders, including lungless salamanders of the family Plethodontidae, which breathe through their skin and the lining of their mouths and lay eggs on land, the young hatching as miniature adults without an aquatic larval stage. The clouded salamander lives in the cavities of decaying logs and even climbs trees. Torrent salamanders, of the genus Rhyacotriton, inhabit cold, clear seeps and headwater streams and are sensitive to warming and sedimentation, making them indicators of intact headwater habitat. The coastal tailed frog, Ascaphus truei, lives in fast, cold mountain streams; its tadpoles use a suction-cup mouth to cling to rocks in swift current, and adult males have a short tail-like extension used in internal fertilization, an unusual trait among frogs. The species belongs to one of the most ancient lineages of living frogs. The rough-skinned newt is common in ponds and forests and carries tetrodotoxin, a potent neurotoxin, in its skin; an evolutionary arms race between these newts and the common garter snakes that prey on them, in which some snake populations have evolved resistance to the toxin, is a classic case study in coevolution.

Southern temperate rainforests have their own remarkable amphibians. Darwin's frogs, Rhinoderma darwinii and its close relative, live in the Valdivian and adjacent forests of Chile and Argentina. Males guard eggs and then take the developing tadpoles into their vocal sacs, where they continue development until they emerge as small froglets, a form of paternal care seen in almost no other vertebrate. Charles Darwin encountered the frog during the voyage of the Beagle, hence the name. One of the two species, the northern Darwin's frog, has not been confirmed for decades and may be extinct, and chytrid fungal disease has been implicated in declines of the surviving species. New Zealand's native frogs, of the genus Leiopelma, are among the most primitive frogs alive, retaining ancestral features and lacking a free-swimming tadpole stage, with some species having froglets carried on the male's back. Several are threatened by introduced predators and disease.

The bird life of temperate rainforests often requires patience, as birds can be difficult to see in the dense canopy. In the Pacific Northwest, the varied thrush delivers its eerie, buzzing single-note song, which seems to hang in the misty air. The Pacific wren, tiny and brown, pours out one of the longest and most complex songs of any North American bird, a cascade of trills from a stump or log. Chestnut-backed chickadees, red-breasted nuthatches, brown creepers, and golden-crowned kinglets forage in the conifers. Pileated woodpeckers excavate large rectangular holes in snags and logs as they hunt carpenter ants, and these excavations later provide homes for other animals. Among the most celebrated and controversial birds are the northern spotted owl and the marbled murrelet. The spotted owl became the focus of intense political conflict in the late twentieth century, when its listing under the United States Endangered Species Act and the subsequent Northwest Forest Plan of 1994 sharply curtailed logging of old-growth forests on federal land. The owl depends heavily on structurally complex old forests, though it now faces an even greater threat from the barred owl, a larger, more aggressive relative that has expanded into its range from the east and competes for territory and prey.

The marbled murrelet is one of the strangest stories in North American ornithology. This small seabird feeds on fish in coastal waters but nests in old-growth forests, sometimes many kilometers inland, laying a single egg directly on a broad, moss-covered branch high in the canopy of a large conifer. For a long time its nesting habits were unknown; the first tree nest in North America was not described until 1974, discovered by a tree climber in California. The murrelet's dependence on old trees with wide, mossy limbs makes it vulnerable to logging, and it is listed as threatened in parts of its range. Its life is an example of how temperate rainforests connect sea and land, much as salmon do, with a bird that commutes daily between the ocean and the canopy.

Southern rainforests offer equally distinctive birds. In Chile, the chucao tapaculo, a small, secretive bird with a rufous breast, calls loudly from the dense understory; in Mapuche tradition its call was used as an omen for travelers depending on which side it was heard from. The Magellanic woodpecker, the largest woodpecker in South America, with males sporting a brilliant red head and crest, depends on mature southern beech forests. The austral parakeet, the southernmost parrot in the world, moves in noisy flocks through beech forests in Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego. In New Zealand, forests are home to birds that evolved in the near-total absence of terrestrial mammals, leading to an unusual number of flightless or ground-dwelling species. The kiwi, nocturnal and probing the forest floor with its long bill bearing nostrils at the tip, is the most famous. The kākā, a forest parrot, and the kererū, a large pigeon that is one of the few remaining birds able to swallow and disperse the largest native fruits, play key ecological roles. The extinction of the giant moa and other large birds after human settlement removed important seed dispersers and browsers, and introduced predators such as stoats, rats, and brushtail possums continue to devastate native bird populations, which is why many New Zealand forests are now the subject of intensive predator-control programs.

Mammals of the temperate rainforest range from tiny to large. In North America, black bears and, in some regions, grizzly bears forage along streams and in berry patches. Roosevelt elk, the largest subspecies of North American elk, browse in the valleys of the Olympic Peninsula and influence the vegetation strongly; their grazing helps maintain the park-like open understory found in parts of the Hoh rainforest. Black-tailed deer, cougars, wolves, bobcats, martens, fishers, and many small rodents complete the picture. On the central coast of British Columbia, the Kermode or spirit bear, a white-coated form of the black bear caused by a recessive gene, is found in notable frequency on certain islands, and research suggests that white bears may be more successful at catching salmon during daylight because fish are less likely to see them against the sky. Coastal wolves in this region feed heavily on salmon and marine resources, swimming between islands.

In southern Chile and Argentina, the mammals are fewer but strange and ancient. The pudú, the world's smallest deer, stands only about thirty-five to forty centimeters at the shoulder and slips through dense bamboo and understory. The kodkod, or güiña, is the smallest wild cat in the Americas. Most remarkable is the monito del monte, Dromiciops gliroides, a small arboreal marsupial that is the only living member of an ancient order, Microbiotheria, and is thought to be more closely related to Australian marsupials than to the opossums of the Americas. It eats insects and fruit, hibernates through winter, and is the principal seed disperser of a mistletoe, Tristerix corymbosus, a relationship so close that the plant's distribution depends on the marsupial. Here again, the ecology of the forest rests on long-standing partnerships between species. In Tasmania, the forests harbor the Tasmanian devil, spotted-tailed quoll, pademelons, and the platypus in streams, as well as bettongs and potoroos that disperse fungal spores.

Invertebrates are less charismatic but equally essential. Beyond the slugs and beetles of the decaying log, rainforest streams support mayflies, stoneflies, and caddisflies whose larvae feed on leaves and algae and in turn feed fish and birds. Glowworms, the larvae of a fungus gnat called Arachnocampa, light up damp banks and caves in New Zealand and parts of Australia, dangling sticky threads to capture insects attracted to their blue-green glow. In Tasmania and Chile, large stag beetles and ancient invertebrate groups occur, including velvet worms, or onychophorans, soft-bodied creatures that shoot sticky slime to capture prey and that represent a lineage stretching back hundreds of millions of years. Finding a velvet worm under a rotting log is a moment of connection with deep time. Tasmanian rainforests also host endemic species of freshwater crayfish, including the giant freshwater crayfish, Astacopsis gouldi, one of the largest freshwater invertebrates in the world, now threatened by habitat degradation and historical overfishing.

Human beings have been part of temperate rainforest ecology for thousands of years, and any account of these forests that leaves out people is incomplete. On the Pacific Northwest coast, Indigenous nations including the Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, Heiltsuk, Nuu-chah-nulth, Coast Salish, and many others developed complex societies supported by salmon, shellfish, plants, and the forest itself. Western redcedar was so central to material culture that it has been called the tree of life; its wood was used for canoes, houses, totem poles, and bentwood boxes, and its bark for clothing, baskets, and rope. Trees from which bark or planks were harvested while the tree remained alive are known as culturally modified trees, and they can be recognized by long rectangular scars or test holes. These trees are documented archaeological features, and in British Columbia many are protected by law. Indigenous management practices, including clam gardens on the shoreline, controlled burning in some areas to promote berries and other foods, and selective harvesting, shaped the landscape in ways that earlier ecologists often failed to recognize. In southern Chile, the Mapuche and Huilliche peoples hold long relationships with forests, including the sacred araucaria or monkey-puzzle tree in the Andean zone, whose seeds, called piñones, have been a traditional food. In New Zealand, Māori knowledge, known as mātauranga Māori, includes deep understanding of forest species and seasons, and in Aotearoa as in Canada, Indigenous-led conservation and co-management arrangements have increasingly shaped how forests are protected.

Industrial logging transformed most temperate rainforests during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. In the Pacific Northwest, the vast majority of original old-growth forest outside protected areas was cut, often by clearcutting, which removes nearly all trees from an area at once. Second-growth forests that regrow after clearcutting tend to be dense, even-aged stands with little dead wood, few snags, and simplified structure; they can take centuries to redevelop old-growth characteristics. Conflicts over remaining old-growth have been among the most significant environmental controversies of recent history. Notable examples include protests in Clayoquot Sound on Vancouver Island in 1993, in which hundreds of people were arrested, the creation of the Great Bear Rainforest agreements on British Columbia's central and north coast, finalized in 2016, which protected a large share of the region's forests through a combination of conservation and ecosystem-based management negotiated with First Nations, and the more recent blockades at Fairy Creek on Vancouver Island beginning in 2020. In Southeast Alaska, the Tongass National Forest, the largest national forest in the United States, has been the subject of decades of debate over roadless area protections and logging. In Tasmania, conflicts over logging of tall forests and rainforests have been fierce, and the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area protects a large portion of the island's remaining wild forests. In Chile, the replacement of native forests with plantations of exotic pine and eucalyptus, encouraged by subsidies beginning in the 1970s, has fragmented the Valdivian rainforest and contributed to increased fire risk.

Even where forests are protected, other pressures continue. Introduced species pose a severe threat in many temperate rainforests.
