The first thing a prospective bookseller learns, usually from another bookseller and usually with a certain rueful pleasure, is that the price is printed on the product. Almost no other retailer lives with this condition. A clothing boutique buys a sweater for forty dollars and decides, according to its neighborhood and its nerve, whether to sell it for ninety or a hundred and twenty. A hardware store sets its own price on a box of screws. The bookseller opens a carton of new hardcovers and finds that the publisher has already decided what each one is worth and has had the figure typeset on the jacket flap. The store can charge less, and its largest competitors routinely do, but it can hardly charge more. Rent may double, the minimum wage may climb, the credit card processor may raise its fees, and the book will still be twenty-nine dollars. Every other fact about the economics of a small bookstore flows downhill from this one.

What the store pays for that book depends on where it comes from. Bought directly from a large publisher, a typical trade title arrives at a discount somewhere around forty-six percent off the list price, sometimes a little better, depending on the terms the publisher offers and the programs the store has joined. Bought from a wholesaler, the same title may come at forty percent or a bit above, with the sacrifice in margin traded for speed and convenience. University press books and technical titles are often sold at what the trade calls short discount, which might be twenty or thirty percent, and which explains why a general bookstore rarely stocks an academic monograph unless a customer has asked for it. Suppose, then, that our twenty-nine-dollar hardcover was bought direct at forty-six percent. The store paid fifteen dollars and sixty-six cents. If the book sells at full price, thirteen dollars and thirty-four cents remains, and from that sum the store must pay for everything else.

Everything else is a formidable category. In a reasonably run small shop, payroll commonly consumes somewhere between twenty and twenty-five percent of sales, and that figure often understates the truth because the owner is not fully paying herself. Rent and associated occupancy costs might take eight to ten percent in a healthy store and fifteen in one that is slowly being suffocated. Card processing takes between two and three percent. Then come utilities, insurance, the point-of-sale system, the website, bags, receipt paper, bookkeeping, marketing, freight on returns, trade association dues, the repair of the door that sticks in August, and the steady small losses to theft and damage. Add these up and it becomes clear why a bookstore that clears two or three percent in net profit is regarded within the industry as doing well. On that twenty-nine-dollar hardcover, a good result is something like seventy cents.

It is worth staying with the seventy cents for a moment, because it changes the way one sees the shop. When a customer asks for a ten percent discount, she is asking for two dollars and ninety cents, which is four times the profit the store hoped to make. When a book is stolen, the store must sell more than twenty similar books to make back the fifteen dollars and sixty-six cents it paid. When a staff member spends half an hour tracking down an obscure paperback for someone who then orders it on his phone while standing at the counter, the store has paid wages for the privilege of serving as a showroom. None of this makes booksellers bitter, or not most of them, but it makes them careful. The romance of the trade is real, and it is sustained by people who know to the penny what it costs.

To understand how a store survives on such margins, one must look at inventory, because inventory is where nearly all the money is. A small general bookstore of fifteen hundred square feet might carry eight to ten thousand titles, with a stock valued at cost somewhere between a hundred thousand and a hundred and fifty thousand dollars. This is, for most owners, the largest single investment of their lives outside of a house, and it sits on shelves gathering sunlight. The central question of the business is how often it turns. If a store carries inventory worth a hundred and twenty thousand dollars at cost and sells books costing three hundred and sixty thousand over the course of a year, its inventory has turned three times, which is a respectable figure. At four turns the store is nimble. At two it is in trouble, or else it is subsidized by someone with another source of income and a love of complete sets.

The arithmetic of turns explains many decisions that puzzle customers. A devoted reader wonders why the shop does not carry all of a certain novelist's eleven books, when she would so happily see them lined up together. The answer is that nine of them would sit for two years apiece, each tying up nine or ten dollars, each occupying an inch of shelf that might have held something that sells every six weeks. Multiply the reader's favorite novelist by three hundred other novelists, each with a devotee of her own, and the store is bankrupt in the midst of plenty. Yet the opposite mistake is just as deadly. A shop that stocks only what turns quickly comes to look like an airport kiosk, and the customer who could buy those same thirty bestsellers at a supermarket for less has no reason to come in. Some slow books earn their keep without selling, because they tell the browser what kind of place this is. A good buyer knows which ones they are and how many she can afford.

Buying, then, is the art at the center of the trade, and it is conducted on a peculiar calendar. Publishers announce their lists in seasons, and a bookseller commonly finds herself in January ordering books for summer, and in May or June committing to the titles on which her Christmas will depend. The traditional instrument for this was the publisher's sales representative, who arrived with a bag of catalogs and a set of well-worn opinions and spent an afternoon in the back room going through the list page by page. Much of that work has moved to digital catalogs, in which a buyer can scroll through hundreds of forthcoming titles, read the rep's notes, look up how the author's last book sold in her own store, and enter her quantities. Yet the good representatives remain valuable, and their value lies in subtraction. A rep who has called on a store for ten years and who says, of a book her own employer is promoting heavily, that it is probably not right for this shop, has purchased a credibility that will later be spent on the odd first novel she truly believes in.

The quantities themselves are tiny. For most new titles a small store will order none. For those it does take, it will usually order one or two copies, perhaps three or four if the author has a following, and ten or twenty for the handful of books expected to dominate a season. The decision between one copy and two seems trivial and is not. A single copy, shelved spine out, may go unnoticed. Two copies can be faced out, so that the cover shows, and when one sells the other remains to keep selling. Five copies can make a small stack on the front table, and a stack announces that the store has made a judgment. But across a thousand titles a season, the difference between an average order of one and a half copies and an average of two amounts to several thousand dollars, and it must be paid for whether or not anyone agrees with the judgment.

What makes this gamble survivable is the second great peculiarity of the trade, which is that the books can be sent back. The practice of returns took hold in American publishing during the Depression, when publishers anxious to persuade frightened booksellers to stock new titles offered to take back what did not sell. It was intended as an emergency inducement and it never went away. Today most trade books from established publishers may be returned for credit, generally after a few months and before the book has been out of print too long, provided they are in salable condition. To outsiders this sounds like a magnificent privilege, and in some respects it is. It allows a shop of modest means to take a chance on a debut poet. It allows the store to bring in eighty copies for an author event and send back forty-five when it rains.

But returns are far from free. Somebody must run the report that identifies which books have not sold, walk the store to pull them, check them for shelf wear, peel off any stickers without tearing the jacket, obtain authorization where it is required, pack them properly, and pay for the freight. A book that has traveled to the store and back again has consumed perhaps two or three dollars in labor and shipping while earning nothing. Returned books come back as credit against future purchases rather than as cash, so that a store hungry for money to pay its rent cannot simply ship its way out of trouble. A store may also find, if its account is past due, that the credit vanishes into the old balance. Still, returns are a tool of cash flow, and experienced booksellers use them with discipline, pulling a section every week so that the task never becomes a catastrophe and so that the shelves keep changing. The rookie's error is sentimental. She keeps the book because she loved it, and loves it, and it remains, and a year later it is too late to send back.

The rhythm of cash is, in fact, the thing that kills bookstores more often than any lack of customers. Publisher invoices are often due in thirty days from the end of the month in which they are issued, which in practice gives the store between one and two months to pay. Books bought in September for the holidays may come due in late October or November, before the customers for whom they were bought have arrived. In response many publishers offer extended dating in the autumn, allowing payment to slide into December or January, and these terms can be the difference between a full shop and a sparse one. The trade's year is badly lopsided. November and December together may account for a quarter to a third of annual sales, with the last ten days before Christmas producing numbers that would be absurd at any other time. A store that takes in twelve hundred dollars on an ordinary Tuesday may take in seven thousand on the Saturday before the holiday.

Then comes January. The register is quiet, the returns are heavy, the bills for the autumn arrive, and there is an unmistakable sensation, in an owner's chest, of a tide going out. A shop that treats its December bank balance as profit discovers by the end of February that most of it belonged to other people. The disciplined owner moves a portion into a separate account as it comes in, labels it with the names of the creditors who will be wanting it, and does not look at it again. She also builds a cash flow projection, which need be nothing grander than a spreadsheet showing what is expected to come in and go out each week for the next three months. It is an unglamorous document. Many owners who have survived a decade will say that it taught them more than any book on their shelves.

Closely related to this is the purchasing budget, known in retail as open-to-buy. The concept is simple. One begins with the sales forecast for a coming month, calculates the cost of the books that will be needed to produce those sales, adjusts for whether inventory is meant to rise or fall, subtracts what has already been ordered, and arrives at the sum still available to spend. A store expecting forty thousand dollars in sales next month, at an average cost of goods of fifty-five percent, will be depleting its shelves by twenty-two thousand dollars at cost. If it wishes to keep inventory level and has fifteen thousand already on order, it may spend seven thousand more. The calculation is easy and the obedience is hard. Every day brings a reason to exceed it, and all of the reasons are books.

The physical logistics begin with the arrival of cartons. A small store may receive anywhere from five to thirty boxes a day depending on the season, from wholesalers whose regional warehouses can often deliver overnight, from the distribution centers of large publishers, and from small presses whose packages come with a handwritten note and an excess of tape. Receiving is the quiet engine of the shop, and it is where a surprising amount of money leaks away. Every carton must be opened, its contents counted against the packing slip, each book scanned into the inventory system, damaged copies set aside and claimed, shortages noted and reported before the window for reporting them closes. Paper is heavy, boxes are handled roughly, and a book with a crushed corner cannot be sold at full price. A store that does not file claims promptly may lose one percent of its purchases to damage and shortage, and one percent of purchases is a large slice of a net profit measured in twos and threes.

Once received, the books must be sorted. Some are special orders, each belonging to a particular customer who must be told that it is here. Some are replacements for copies sold yesterday. Some are new titles that must appear on the front table, though certain of them may not appear yet, because they are under embargo until a fixed release date, usually a Tuesday, and the store has signed an affidavit promising not to sell them early. The rest go into sections, and in each section something must usually move to make room. Shelving is slow, and done well it is also a form of study. The bookseller who shelves the history section every week knows, without consulting the computer, that the new biography has not budged and that there is a hole where the old one used to be.

The inventory system deserves its own word of respect. A modern bookstore's point-of-sale software does far more than ring up purchases. It holds a record for each title, remembers when every copy arrived and sold, suggests reorders, tracks special orders, manages customer accounts, stores gift card balances, and feeds the website with a current picture of what is in stock. It costs a small store perhaps a hundred and fifty to four hundred dollars a month, and it is worth this only to the degree that its data can be believed. If the computer says there is one copy of a novel on the shelf and there is none, then the computer will not suggest reordering it, the website will promise it to a stranger, and a bookseller will spend ten minutes hunting for a ghost. Such phantoms accumulate through theft, misshelving, and careless scanning. The annual physical inventory, in which the store counts everything it owns, is dreaded, conducted late at night with the help of pizza, and absolutely necessary.

Whether to order direct from publishers or through a wholesaler is a daily question with no permanent answer. Direct buying offers better margin, but it may involve minimum orders, slower delivery, and a separate invoice, account, and return procedure for each of dozens of vendors. A wholesaler offers nearly everything in one box the next day or the day after. A sensible store uses publishers for its frontlist and for large backlist replenishments, waiting until an order is big enough to earn free freight and the best terms, and uses the wholesaler for special orders, sudden demand, and small presses that would not otherwise be worth the paperwork. Five points of margin across a year's purchases can be worth fifteen or twenty thousand dollars to a shop with four hundred thousand in sales. That is the salary of a part-time employee, or the whole of the profit. But a book that is out of stock for nine days while waiting for the direct shipment has a margin of zero.

Because the margin on books is constrained, nearly every independent bookstore sells other things. The trade calls them sidelines, or non-book, and they include greeting cards, journals, puzzles, candles, tote bags, socks, mugs, and small toys. A card bought for two dollars and sold for five earns sixty percent, takes up little room, and is purchased by people who came in for something else. Non-book merchandise may make up fifteen to twenty-five percent of sales in a typical shop, and a greater share of gross profit. Purists complain, and the owner has learned to smile at them. The candles, she might say, are paying for the poetry. There is nonetheless a limit, rarely marked, beyond which a bookstore with gifts becomes a gift shop with books, and customers sense the crossing before the owner does. Sidelines also have their own hazard, for they generally cannot be returned. The ceramic hedgehogs, if they were a mistake, are a permanent one.

Used books provide a different sort of relief. A used paperback acquired for two dollars in store credit and sold for eight yields a margin that new books can never approach, and it brings people in, both to sell and to browse. Against this must be set the labor of sorting, the cost of cleaning and pricing, the endless diplomacy of declining a grandfather's encyclopedias, and the space. No one sends a catalog of used books. The store must take what comes through the door, judge it in a few seconds, and live with the result. Shops that combine new and used successfully usually have somebody on staff with a genuine talent for this judgment, and they tend to set firm rules about when they buy and how much credit may be spent on new stock, lest the store find that it has been paying cash for books and accepting paper for them.

A café is the sideline that everyone suggests. Customers imagine it, friends urge it, and landlords have opinions. Coffee does carry a splendid gross margin, and it lengthens the visit. But it is also a second business, with its own equipment, permits, health inspections, spoilage, training, and rhythm of rushes. An espresso machine may cost as much as a year's purchases from a midsize publisher, and it requires someone to stand behind it whether or not anyone is thirsty. Stores that make it work generally do enough volume to keep that person busy, or else rent the space to an independent operator and let the steam be somebody else's problem. A shop of a thousand square feet with two employees is usually better off next door to a good café than containing a poor one.

Then there is the matter of place. A bookstore needs foot traffic, yet the streets with the most foot traffic charge rents that books cannot support. The owner who signs a lease is making what may be the most consequential decision of the whole enterprise, and she is often doing so against a counterparty who has signed a hundred. Beyond the headline rent lie the shared costs of taxes, insurance, and maintenance that are passed through under a triple net lease, and which can add a quarter or more to the monthly bill. Beyond those lie the annual escalations, the question of who replaces a dead air conditioner, the personal guarantee, and the renewal option. A bookstore builds value slowly, through years of habit, and a lease without a renewal option hands that value to the landlord at the end of the term. Some of the saddest closings in the trade have involved busy, beloved shops whose sales were rising as the moving trucks arrived.

For this reason the most secure independent bookstores are often those that own their buildings, sometimes through the foresight of a founder who bought a storefront when the block was shabby. Such owners may joke that they are in the real estate business and merely decorate the premises with literature. Those who cannot buy have tried other arrangements. Some have persuaded communities to invest, raising loans from hundreds of customers in modest amounts. Some have reorganized as cooperatives, with members owning shares, or have moved part of their work, usually school programs and events, into a nonprofit entity that can receive donations. A few have found landlords who accept a lower rent because a bookstore makes the apartments upstairs more desirable. Each of these has its complications, but together they reflect a recognition that the value a bookstore gives to a neighborhood is larger than what it can collect at the register.

Inside the space, layout is economics made visible. The area just within the door is a zone of decompression, where entering customers adjust their eyes and notice little. The first table beyond it is the most valuable square yardage in the shop, and what rests on it is examined by nearly everyone. Children's books are usually placed at the back, so that families pass the whole store on the way and so that noise is contained there. The register wants to be where a bookseller can see the entrance and greet people. Shelves in the middle of the floor should be low enough to see across, which makes the store feel larger and theft harder, and they are better on wheels, so that they can be rolled aside when forty chairs must be set out. Lighting matters enormously. So does the presence of a chair, or the absence of one, about which booksellers hold opinions of theological intensity.

Display is the cheapest form of marketing a store possesses. A book shown face out will typically sell far better than the same book spine out, and a book with a handwritten card beneath it, signed by a member of the staff, will sell better still. These cards, called shelf talkers, are small marvels of commerce. A few sincere sentences from a bookseller named on the card can move a hundred copies over a year of a ten-year-old novel that no one is advertising, and those sales are nearly pure improvement, since they were generated from within the shop. Every successful independent has a few such titles, books that it sells in quantities wildly out of proportion to its size because somebody there cannot stop talking about them. This practice is called handselling, and it is the closest thing the trade has to a secret weapon. An algorithm can report what other people bought. A bookseller can ask what you loved last and watch your face while you answer.

That ability lives in the staff, and the staff is where the economics become moral as well as arithmetical. Bookselling attracts educated, curious, overqualified people, and it has historically paid them poorly, on the unstated theory that proximity to books is a form of compensation. It is not a form that landlords accept. A shop open sixty hours a week, with two people on the floor at most times, requires a hundred and twenty staffed hours before anyone has received a shipment, written a newsletter, or balanced the books. At eighteen dollars an hour, with payroll taxes added, those hours alone come to roughly a hundred and twenty thousand dollars a year, which is the whole payroll budget of a store selling half a million dollars' worth of goods. There is no slack in these numbers. A dollar an hour more, given gladly and deserved plainly, costs over six thousand dollars, and it must come from additional sales of nearly fifteen thousand.

Owners respond to this squeeze in several ways, of which the commonest is to work for nothing themselves. The unpaid owner is the hidden subsidy of independent bookselling, and it distorts every figure the business produces. A shop showing a profit of twelve thousand dollars on the strength of fifty-five free hours a week is not profitable at all; it has simply found an investor who accepts exhaustion as a dividend. This can be endured in the first year or two, when the enterprise is gathering its strength, but it makes a poor foundation. It conceals bad decisions, it prevents the store from being sold to anyone who needs an income, and it ends, as often as not, with a sign in the window thanking the community for many wonderful years. The better practice is to enter an owner's salary in the budget from the beginning, even a small one, and to regard failure to pay it as a problem to be solved.

Events are another part of the business where the visible and the actual diverge. From the audience an author reading looks like the purest expression of what a bookstore is for, and perhaps it is. From behind the counter it looks like six weeks of work. The store must pitch the publicist or be pitched, settle a date, order the books in a quantity that is always a guess, design a poster, write the listing, post it in a dozen places, remind the local paper, stay open late, move the furniture, test the microphone, introduce the author, sell the books, clean the floor, and return whatever remains. If twelve people come and five buy a book, the gross profit is about sixty-five dollars, and the store has spent perhaps three hundred in wages. If two hundred come and a hundred and forty buy, the evening pays for a good many of the others.

Since no one can predict reliably which it will be, stores have learned to reduce the risk. Many now sell tickets to larger events, with the price including the book, so that attendance becomes revenue. They hold big occasions in libraries, churches, and theaters, where chairs already exist. They pair a little-known author with a well-known local one, since the surest predictor of a crowd is the number of friends the author has within driving distance. And they count benefits beyond the night's receipts, including the mailing list that grows, the publisher who notices that the store can draw, and the fellow who came reluctantly with his wife and returns alone the following Saturday. These benefits are real. They are also the sort of benefits that can be used to excuse anything, and a prudent owner reviews the year's events and cancels the kinds that have never once paid.

Much of the sturdier revenue comes from outside the walls. Schools are the great example. A book fair, at which a store brings several thousand dollars' worth of children's titles to a school library for a week, can produce as much as a slow fortnight in the shop, though the school receives a share of the proceeds and the boxes must be carried both ways. Author visits to schools, with order forms sent home beforehand, may sell two or three hundred copies in a morning. Local businesses buy books for conferences and training, organizations need them for speakers, and libraries will sometimes purchase from a nearby shop if the discount and paperwork are tolerable. Bulk orders usually demand a lower price, but they require no shelf space, no browsing, and often no inventory risk whatever. An order of two hundred copies sold at fifteen percent off may look thin on paper and yet leave more behind than a week of ordinary trade.

Book clubs provide a gentler version of the same thing. A shop that registers thirty local clubs, stocks their selections, and gives members a small discount has thirty groups of eight or ten people with a monthly reason to come through the door. Subscription programs go further, sending a chosen book each month to customers who pay in advance. Here the economics are nearly ideal, for the cash arrives first, the quantity is known, and the selection rests on the very expertise that distinguishes the store. A subscription of two hundred members at thirty dollars a month is seventy-two thousand dollars in annual revenue that does not depend on the weather. It also requires that someone wrap and ship two hundred parcels every month, choose a book that two hundred different people do not already own, and answer their messages when the parcel goes astray.

Shipping brings us to the website, and to the large shadow that falls across any discussion of bookselling. The dominant online retailer sells books in immense variety, frequently at a discount that a small store could not match without losing money on every copy, and delivers them quickly to the door. It is able to do so because books are for it a minor part of a vast enterprise, useful for acquiring customers, and because it extracts from publishers terms commensurate with its size. No independent can win on price or on selection, and the ones that have tried are gone. The survivors compete on other ground. They offer discovery instead of search, a few thousand books that someone has thought about rather than millions that no one has, and a room where a person may spend an unhurried hour among strangers without being asked to justify it.

Still, customers expect to be able to order online, and the pandemic year of 2020 turned that expectation into a necessity almost overnight. Shops that had treated their websites as brochures found themselves running small warehouses, with booksellers in masks packing mailers until midnight. Platforms arose or expanded to help, some of them letting a store earn a commission on orders fulfilled directly from a wholesaler. A commission of around thirty percent of list price, with no inventory, labor, or postage, compares well with the forty-odd percent earned on a book that the store must buy, hold, pack, and mail. Shipping from the shop itself is more personal but seldom lucrative. Media mail is cheap but slow, a padded envelope and label cost something, ten minutes of packing costs more, and a customer accustomed to free delivery will balk at paying five dollars for it. Many shops have concluded that the best online order is one the customer comes in to collect, since she rarely leaves with only that book.

Audiobooks and electronic books occupy a smaller place. Services exist that allow an independent to share in the revenue from digital audio, and a store that promotes them steadily can build a modest stream of monthly income that arrives with scarcely any effort. The margins in dollars are slight, but the point is partly defensive. A customer who listens during her commute is going to buy from somebody, and it is better that her monthly credit support the shop she likes than the company she feels vaguely guilty about. Electronic books, once expected to extinguish the printed kind altogether, settled into a share of the market that leaves print clearly predominant in most categories the independents care about. The obituaries written for the bookstore in the first decade of this century have not aged well. In the United States, the number of independent stores belonging to the national association fell sharply through the nineties and the early two-thousands, reached its low point around 2009, and has since recovered strongly, with a great many new openings after 2020.

It would be wrong to read that recovery as proof that the business has become easy. New stores open partly because they can be opened on a smaller scale than before. Some begin as pop-ups, carts, or converted vans, testing an audience before committing to a lease. Some specialize, in romance, or mysteries, or cookbooks, or books for children, or literature in translation, gaining in intensity what they give up in breadth. Romance stores have been an instructive case, because their customers read voraciously, buy in series, travel considerable distances, and talk to one another continually online. A specialist shop can know its field more deeply than any generalist, stock it more efficiently, and become a destination. It also ties its fortunes to a single taste, and tastes shift.

A person determined to open a general shop should expect to need more money than she first supposes. Opening inventory for a store of twelve hundred square feet may cost seventy-five to a hundred thousand dollars, though some suppliers offer extended terms on opening orders that soften the blow. Shelving and fixtures might take twenty to forty thousand, less if bought secondhand from a store that is closing, which is a melancholy but thrifty custom. There are deposits, permits, signs, computers, paint, electrical work, legal advice, insurance, and a launch. Above all there must be working capital, a reserve sufficient to cover several months of expenses while the neighborhood learns that the store exists. It is this last item that optimistic plans omit. The shelves are filled, the ribbon is cut, the party is glorious, and there remains four thousand dollars in the bank with a slow spring ahead.

Publishers and wholesalers, for their part, must be persuaded to extend credit to a business without a history. A new store may have to prepay at first, or offer a personal guarantee, or operate beneath a low credit limit that constrains its first holiday season just when stock is most needed. Trust is built by paying on time, and where that proves impossible, by calling before the due date rather than hiding from the phone after it. Credit managers have heard everything, and they generally prefer an honest schedule of partial payments to an eloquent silence. A store placed on hold by a large publisher cannot receive that publisher's books, which means that it cannot sell them, which means that it cannot earn the money to be taken off hold. That spiral is among the most common ways for a shop to die, and it is visible on the shelves months ahead, in the gaps.

Customers see those gaps, even if they cannot name them, and this is why experienced owners in difficulty cut almost anything before they cut the stock. A thinning bookstore sells less, and selling less, thins further. The better remedy is to rebalance. One returns what is dead, concentrates the remaining money on sections that are turning, faces out more titles to keep the shelves looking generous, shortens the hours that bring in little, and examines every recurring bill. It is remarkable how often a shop in distress is paying for a forgotten service, a second telephone line, or a copier lease that nobody remembers signing. It is equally remarkable how often a store is losing money in one identifiable place, such as a Monday evening or an overgrown section of reference books, and how long it can take its owner to look.

Measuring by section is a useful habit for that reason. A store can compare the share of its inventory represented by each category with the share of sales it produces. If children's books are twenty percent of the stock and thirty-two percent of the sales, they are starved for room. If travel occupies eight percent of the stock and yields three percent of the sales, then the guidebooks to distant capitals are living on the charity of the picture books. Numbers of this kind should not govern absolutely. A poetry section may lag forever and still belong, since it costs little and its readers are loyal. But the decision to carry it at a loss ought to be a decision, made with open eyes, rather than a thing that has merely happened.

Theft should be mentioned, because it surprises people who believe that readers are honest. Many are, but shrinkage in a small shop commonly runs near one percent of sales and can run higher. Certain authors are stolen so consistently that stores keep their works behind the counter, and booksellers exchange the names with grim amusement. The best prevention is not a camera but a greeting. A person who has been looked at and spoken to is less likely to slip a paperback into a coat, and an honest person who has been greeted is more likely to buy one. Like so much in retail, the measure that protects the store turns out to be the same as the measure that makes it pleasant.

The community around a bookstore is often described in warm and foggy language, but it has an economic structure too. A typical shop does a large portion of its business with a small portion of its customers, people who visit weekly, buy gifts nowhere else, and bring visiting relatives in as though to a local monument. Losing ten such households would hurt more than losing two hundred occasional visitors. Loyalty programs try to recognize them, usually with some credit after a certain amount of spending, and these programs must be designed with care, because a reward worth five percent of sales is larger than the profit of many stores. What these customers value most, in any case, can be given at no cost. They like to be remembered. They like it when the bookseller says that something came in yesterday which made her think of them.

There is also the matter of what a store chooses to stand for. Every selection is a kind of argument, and in recent years arguments over books have grown heated, with challenges to titles in schools and libraries and pressures from several directions on what shops display. An independent has the freedom to stock what it believes in and the exposure that goes with that freedom. Some have found that taking a visible position deepens the loyalty of their customers. Others, especially in small towns where the shop must serve everyone, have quietly built shelves on which neighbors who disagree may each find something and perhaps something of the other's. Neither approach is free of cost, and no spreadsheet settles the question.

Eventually each owner faces the question of how to leave. An independent bookstore is an awkward thing to sell. Its inventory has a value, its name has a value in the affections of the town, and its modest earnings support only a modest price. A typical sale might fetch the cost of the stock, adjusted for what is stale, plus a little for fixtures and goodwill. The most promising buyer is frequently already in the shop, shelving the biographies, and lacks only money. Thoughtful owners begin years ahead, teaching a manager to read the financial statements, letting her do the buying for a season, and arranging for the purchase to be paid gradually from the store's own proceeds. Those who wait for a stranger with a check often wait too long, and then there is a closing sale, with everyone in town coming at last to say how much they loved the place.

That remark, heard so often at closings, contains the whole problem. Affection does not appear on an income statement until it is converted into purchases, and a bookstore that is widely loved and seldom used will fail in an atmosphere of general esteem. The shops that endure have found ways to make the conversion easy and frequent. They remind people, without scolding, that the gift they need by Friday is here, that any book can be ordered, that the school list has been stocked, that the new one by that author arrives on Tuesday. They do not ask to be treated as a charity. They ask to be treated as a habit.

Consider, finally, an ordinary weekday in such a place. The owner arrives at eight, two hours before opening, and pays three invoices while the coffee brews. The delivery comes at half past nine, eleven cartons, one with a split side. By ten a bookseller has received four of them and called five customers about special orders. The morning is slow. A retired teacher buys a mystery and stays to discuss it, a courier asks for directions, and a mother with a stroller sits on the floor of the children's section and reads the same picture book aloud three times before buying it. At noon the owner eats a sandwich over a digital catalog, deciding between one copy and two. In the afternoon a school calls to ask for ninety copies of a novel by the end of next week, and the day is transformed. By closing the register shows sixteen hundred dollars, not counting the school, which is better than last year.

If all the sums come out as they should, the store will keep perhaps forty or fifty dollars of that day's receipts, and some of it will go toward the door that sticks. Measured against the hours and the capital, it is a poor return, and anyone seeking only a return would be well advised to put the money elsewhere and visit bookstores as a customer. Yet it would be a mistake to conclude that the economics are therefore beside the point, or that those who love the work must hold their noses and endure the numbers. The numbers are how the work continues. Each careful order, each claim filed, each carton returned in time, each lease read to its last page is what allows the lights to be on when some child wanders past the front table and into the back, and sits down, and opens something. The seventy cents is small, but it is what keeps the door unlocked, and in the morning the cartons come again.
